question: Which AI practices are prohibited?
answer: The Act prohibits: (i) AI systems that deploy subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort a person’s behaviour and impair informed decision‑making [3]; (ii) AI systems that detect or infer emotions or intentions from biometric data in workplace or education settings, except when used strictly for medical or safety purposes [1]; (iii) AI systems that make risk assessments predicting a natural person’s likelihood of committing a criminal offence solely on profiling or personality traits, unless they only support a human assessment based on objective facts [2]; (iv) AI systems that create or expand facial‑recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage [2]; and (v) AI systems that infer emotions of natural persons in the workplace (as part of the same prohibition) [2].

question: When do the prohibitions on AI practices start to apply?
answer: The prohibitions on AI practices are intended to start applying from 2 February 2025 [1].

question: What must providers of high-risk AI systems do about risk management?
answer: Providers must put in place a risk‑management system that identifies reasonably foreseeable misuse of the high‑risk AI system and any resulting health, safety or fundamental‑rights risks, documents the choices made and, where relevant, involves experts and external stakeholders [1]. They must test the system throughout development and at least once before it is placed on the market, using predefined metrics and thresholds to determine the most appropriate risk‑management measures [3]. The adopted measures must be targeted, able to be mitigated or eliminated through design or technical information, and take into account the combined effect of all regulatory requirements [5]. All of this must be recorded in a documented quality‑management system that includes policies, procedures and instructions [2].

question: What requirements apply to the training data of high-risk AI systems?
answer: The training (as well as validation and testing) data sets must be of high quality – relevant, sufficiently representative and, as far as possible, free of errors – and be managed under appropriate data‑governance practices [1]. These practices must address the design choices, collection processes and origin of the data (including the original purpose for personal data), all preparation steps (annotation, labeling, cleaning, enrichment, etc.), the assumptions behind the data, and an assessment of the data’s availability, quantity and suitability [3]. Providers must also examine the data for biases that could affect health, safety or fundamental rights [3]. The documentation accompanying the system must specify the input‑data requirements and any relevant information about the training, validation and testing data sets used [4].

question: What must the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system contain?
answer: The technical documentation of a high‑risk AI system must be prepared before the system is placed on the market, kept up‑to‑date, and presented in a clear, comprehensive form that demonstrates compliance with the Act [3]. It must detail the system’s performance for the specific persons or groups it is intended to serve, the specifications of the input data and of the training, validation and testing data sets, and provide information that enables deployers to correctly interpret the system’s outputs [4]. It must also describe any pre‑determined changes to the system and its performance, the human‑oversight measures (including technical measures to aid interpretation), the computational and hardware resources required, the expected lifetime of the system and any necessary maintenance or care [4].

question: How must high-risk AI systems allow for human oversight?
answer: High‑risk AI systems must be designed and developed with built‑in operational constraints and appropriate human‑machine‑interface tools that cannot be overridden by the system, so that natural persons can effectively monitor, interpret and intervene in its operation throughout its lifecycle【2】. The provider must identify suitable human‑oversight measures before the system is placed on the market, ensuring that the system guides and informs the assigned human operator to make informed decisions about when and how to intervene or stop the system【1】. The system must be supplied in a way that enables the overseer, who has the necessary competence, training and authority, to understand its capacities and limitations, detect anomalies, avoid automation bias and correctly interpret its outputs【5】.

question: Must people be told that they are interacting with an AI system such as a chatbot?
answer: Yes. The Act requires that natural persons be notified when they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well‑informed, observant and circumspect person, and the notification must consider vulnerable groups such as children or persons with disabilities【1】.

question: What obligations do providers of general-purpose AI models have?
answer: Providers of general‑purpose AI models must draw up and keep up‑to‑date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing processes and evaluation results, and make this documentation available to the AI Office and national competent authorities on request [3]. They must also keep up‑to‑date and provide information and documentation to providers of AI systems that intend to integrate the model [3]. In addition, they must cooperate with the Commission and national competent authorities and may rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published [2]. If the model is classified as having systemic risk, the provider must additionally perform standardized model evaluation and adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level, report serious incidents and corrective measures, and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity [4]. These obligations do not apply to models released under a free and open‑source licence unless they present systemic risks [2][5].

question: How does the AI Act define an AI system?
answer: The Act defines an “AI system” as a machine‑based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, which may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from its inputs how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments【1】.

question: Which areas are listed as high-risk AI use cases?
Who must ensure AI literacy, and what does it involve?
answer: Providers and deployers of AI systems must ensure AI literacy. They are required to take measures that give their staff and any persons operating or using the systems on their behalf a sufficient level of AI literacy, adapted to the individuals’ technical knowledge, experience, education, training and the specific context of use, as well as to the persons or groups affected by the system [5]. AI literacy is intended to provide all relevant actors in the AI value chain with the insights needed to understand how AI‑driven decisions impact them and to ensure appropriate compliance with the Regulation’s rights, risks and safeguards [1].

question: What is an AI regulatory sandbox?
answer: An AI regulatory sandbox is a controlled framework established by a competent authority that allows providers or prospective providers of AI systems to develop, train, validate and test innovative AI systems—potentially in real‑world conditions—under regulatory supervision for a limited time and according to an agreed sandbox plan [3]. It is intended to facilitate development and testing of such systems before they are placed on the market, while ensuring strict oversight of risks to fundamental rights, health and safety [1].

question: When is a general-purpose AI model considered to have systemic risk?
answer: A general‑purpose AI model is regarded as presenting systemic risk when its high‑impact capabilities can cause a significant impact on the Union market or lead to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights or society as a whole, and these effects can be propagated at scale across the value chain [3]. The Commission may also designate a model as having systemic risk ex officio or on a qualified alert, based on the criteria set out in Annex XIII [5].

question: Yüksek riskli yapay zeka sistemlerinde insan gözetimi nasıl sağlanmalı?
answer: Yüksek riskli AI sistemlerinde insan gözetimi, sağlayıcı tarafından sistemin piyasaya sürülmeden önce tanımlanmalı ve sistemin kendisi tarafından devredilemeyen yerleşik operasyonel kısıtlamalar içermelidir; gözetimi yapacak doğal kişilerin gerekli yetkinlik, eğitim ve yetkiye sahip olması gerekir [1]. Sistem, uygun insan‑makine arayüz araçlarıyla tasarlanmalı ve kullanım süresince doğal kişilerin etkili bir şekilde denetleyebilmesini sağlamalıdır; bu gözetim, sağlık, güvenlik ve temel haklara yönelik riskleri önlemeyi veya en aza indirmeyi amaçlar [2]. Sağlayıcı, gözetim görevlilerine sistemin kapasite ve sınırlamalarını anlamaları, anormallikleri tespit etmeleri, otomasyon yanlılığına karşı uyanık olmaları ve çıktıyı doğru yorumlamaları için gerekli bilgi ve araçları sunmalıdır [3]. Deployörler, bu görevleri yerine getirecek kişileri yetkinlik, eğitim ve otorite bakımından seçmeli ve onlara gerekli desteği sağlamalıdır [4].

question: Deepfake içeriklerin yapay zeka ile üretildiği belirtilmek zorunda mı?
answer: Evet, derin‑fake (deep‑fake) olarak nitelendirilen yapay zeka tarafından üretilen veya değiştirilmiş görüntü, ses ya da video içeriklerinin yapay olarak oluşturulduğu ya da değiştirildiği açıkça belirtilmelidir【1】【2】. Bu şeffaflık yükümlülüğü, içeriğin sanat, yaratıcılık, hiciv, kurgu vb. bir eser içinde yer alması durumunda, eserin gösterimini veya keyfini engellemeyecek şekilde yalnızca varlığının bildirilmesiyle sınırlanabilir【1】【2】. Ayrıca, suçun tespiti, önlenmesi, soruşturulması veya kovuşturulması amacıyla yasal olarak yetkilendirilmiş kullanımlarda bu yükümlülük uygulanmaz【2】.

question: Yasaklı yapay zeka uygulamaları için en yüksek para cezası nedir?
answer: Yasaklı yapay zeka uygulamaları için uygulanabilecek en yüksek para cezası, yıllık toplam küresel cirosunun % 3’ü ya da 15 milyon € tutarından hangisi daha yüksekse o kadar olabilir [3].
